what_it_does: Quantum computers store information in qubits, which are supposed to live in two states (0 and 1), but physical qubits can accidentally escape into higher-energy states (called leakage), turning them into silent saboteurs that corrupt every error-detection cycle until they are reset. The problem is that the main data qubits are never measured directly during normal operation, so detecting leakage is hard. GLADIATOR is a system that watches the pattern of indirect measurement signals (called syndrome bits) each cycle, consults a precomputed probability table to decide whether leakage is the most likely explanation, and only applies the expensive reset operation when it is — reducing unnecessary resets by up to 3x and cutting overall error rates by 16%.
method_in_detail:
The problem with naive detection. The prior state-of-the-art system (called ERASER) used a simple rule: if 50% or more of the parity-check bits connected to a data qubit flip in one cycle, that qubit is probably leaked, so reset it. The trouble is that ordinary gate errors (which happen about 10x more often than leakage) can produce the same patterns. ERASER flagged 11 out of 16 possible 4-bit syndrome patterns as leakage, causing massive false alarms.

The idea. GLADIATOR reframes leakage detection as a graph-labeling problem. Before the quantum computer runs, an offline analysis step builds two weighted graphs — one describing how leakage causes syndrome patterns to evolve over time, one describing how ordinary gate errors do the same. Each node in the graph is a syndrome pattern (e.g., '1001'); each directed edge carries a probability weight derived from real device calibration data. By summing incoming edge weights from the leakage graph versus the non-leakage graph for every node, GLADIATOR labels each pattern as 'leakage-dominated' or not, and writes the result into a small lookup table.

How it runs in real time. During each error-correction cycle (which lasts roughly 1 microsecond on a superconducting chip), a small circuit called the Data-Parity Adjacency Generator collects the flipped syndrome bits associated with each data qubit and forms a 5-bit code. That code is checked against the precomputed Boolean logic in under 1 nanosecond — using at most 10 lookup-table units (tiny programmable logic cells) per data qubit on an FPGA. If the pattern matches a leakage signature, the system triggers a reset; otherwise it does nothing.

The key design choice. By building the decision logic offline from physics-calibrated probabilities rather than hard-coding a threshold, GLADIATOR adapts to different quantum error-correcting codes (surface codes, color codes, qLDPC codes) just by rebuilding the graph — no structural changes needed. An extended version (GLADIATOR-D) watches two consecutive cycles before deciding, further cutting false positives.

The result. Versus ERASER, GLADIATOR uses 17x to 80x fewer FPGA resources, reduces false positive resets by ~1.9x, lowers residual qubit leakage by ~1.7x, and shortens the effective error-correction cycle by 1.7x to 3.9x across tested code types.
